name: Garo
confidence_why: Burling's 2004 reference grammar of Modhupur Mandi and his 1981 article both place Garo's weak, non-contrastive stress on the final syllable of the stem, drawn onto most verb suffixes and the plural and reflexive noun suffixes but not onto case clitics, and the only dissent is a one-clause aside in Duanmu 1994 calling the stress "probably trochaic" on Burling's personal communication, with no data behind it.

new_statements.quote: In addition to lacking tone, Garo lacks anything like the contrastive, or nearly contrastive, word stress of English. [...] To the extent that Garo can be said to have stress at all, it is relatively independent of the segmental phonology and relatively closely tied to the larger patterns of intonation. [...] The first generalization about stress is that when bisyllabic nouns without suffixes are pronounced in isolation, and in the least emphatic or least marked fashion, they have a mild stress on the second syllable. [...] the strongest stress also seems to fall on the final syllable in nouns of more than two syllables.

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Garo with an empty rule; this source supplies the placement (final syllable of the stem/word, non-contrastive, with the suffix exceptions above), so it refines rather than agrees or contradicts. the Internet Archive text of the SPO edition; pagination is the SPO edition's ('Page 59' markers), which may differ from the 2004 Bibliophile print edition.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is weak, non-contrastive and tied to intonation; Burling says it mainly delimits word boundaries ('what I will call "stress" helps to define the boundaries of a word', p. 58). In unmarked isolated pronunciation the main stress falls on the final syllable of the stem: bisyllabic nouns are stressed on the second syllable (bi-gíl 'skin'), longer nouns and compounds on the final syllable, numerals on the number (final syllable), reduplicated adverbs on the last syllable, verbs on the last derivational/inflectional/tense suffix (kam-prú-a, kat-píl-a, kat-ang-na-jók). Phonetically a slight pitch rise then fall, probably a bit longer and louder. Case clitics and a few suffixes do not attract stress, so stress stays on the stem-final syllable (na-chíl-o).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Yes, weaker stress on the first syllable of 1+2 compounds: 'Such words have heaviest stress on the final syllable, somewhat weaker stress on the first, and the least on the second' (bòl-bi-ják 'tree leaf', p. 59); first members of compounds keep something of their own pattern (pi-pròt-ki'-sáng); reduplicated adverbs keep 'some residual stress.. at the end of the first half' (hèng-e-héng-e, p. 65); a weak stress remains on -ja- in dak-jà-ing-jók (p. 62).
new_statements.exceptions: Suffixes that do NOT attract stress (stress stays on the preceding stem-final syllable): case clitics locative -o, accusative -ko, possessive -ni, instrumental -cha; -ra-ra; neutral tense -a; progressive -ing- (stress 'jumps over' it to a following tense suffix); subordinating -e / -e-ming; nominalizing -gip-a / -a; nominative -a of pronouns; -na quotative, -ma question, -ming past/conditional. Suffixes that DO attract stress: plural -drang, reflexive -tang, all derivational suffixes, most inflectional suffixes (last one wins), tense-aspect -jok, -na-jok, -no-a (on -no-, not -a), -kon 'probably'. Closed syllables seem to attract stress more decisively than open ones (an uninvestigated 'hunch', p. 61). Author repeatedly flags the description as partial and impressionistic.
new_statements.identity_note: Burling's grammar describes the Mandi dialect of Modhupur (Tangail district, Bangladesh), with regular comparison to A'chik, the standard Garo of the Garo Hills (e.g. future -no-a is 'in the Mandi dialect'; the negative-question intonation is flagged as possibly Mandi-only). The stress section is written as applying to Garo generally. Chainary & Basumatary describe Garo generically, noting the A'we dialect is the current standard.

new_statements.quote: The derivational suffixes uniformly draw the stress to themselves and away from the preceding verb root. Thus: ré'-a 'go, come', re'-áng-a 'go away', kám-a 'burn', kam-prú-a 'burn through', ní-a 'look', ni-tát-a 'stare'. This pattern of stress on the final syllable applies to a very large number of verb stems. [...] other case suffixes such as the accusative -ko, the possessive -ni, and the instrumental -cha also tend to leave the stress, on the previous syllable. [...] This means that in all cases the stress falls on the final syllable of the numeral, just before the case suffix if there is one.
